newsitem.title: USA: FUND VIEW - Oakmark Small Cap avoids tech stocks.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Oakmark Small Cap avoids tech stocks.

text.p: Want to rank first in performance among small cap mutual funds? Don't buy technology stocks, advised Steven Reid, portfolio manager of the Oakmark Small Cap Fund.

"We have no technology," Reid told Reuters. "We never got involved. We think of investing as more of a marathon than a sprint...Technology today is obsolete tomorrow. Product life cycles for hard goods and services is much shorter than our (investment) horizon of three to five years."

The strategy appears to be working. According to Lipper Analytical Services, the fund has returned 8.93 percent year to date, making it first among 437 funds in the sector, where the average return is off 1.94 percent.
In 1996, Oakmark returned 39.79 percent, ranking it 14th. The average return was 20.01 percent.
Reid favors the bottoms up, value approach, seeking individual securities that are undervalued, especially when putting price tags on assets.
One general sector that Reid likes is restructuring-related spinoffs.
The fund's largest holding is US Industries Inc, which comprises about seven percent of the $570 million fund.

US Industries, which was spun off by Hanson Plc HNSN.L in 1995, was expected to reduce debt to $500 million this September from $1.5 billion and has reduced its number of businesses, either through sales or combinations.

"It had almost 35 different businesses, and that's what scared away Wall Street," Reid said. "There was too much to try to understand. The reality is that debt covenants require it to trim the company down and form a core group of businesses."
Some of the better known businesses include Jacuzzi, Ames handtools, Farberware cookware and Scott golf clubs.
Another bonus: It is repurchasing shares. The stock gained 1/8 to 36-5/8, near its 12-month high of 36-7/8.

Another spinoff Reid likes is Catellus Development Corp, at 5.3 percent of the portfolio. Catellus, spun out of the old Sante Fe Pacific Corp railroad, is the largest landowner in California, with the industrial and commercial properties located near major transportation systems.
New managers have "done a first-rate job in managing assets," he said. Shares rose 3/8 to 15-5/8.
Another big holding is SPX Corp at 6.25 percent, which makes specialty service tools and original equipment components for the motor vehicle industry.
The company brought in new management, which is "very share incentified. They've done a tremendous job building a culture that is performance based," Reid said.

Reid said the company has "strategically sold undeperforming businesses and reduced debt per share by $25. It's really dramatic. The stock is underfollowed, and underappreciated. It's pretty ripe territory." Shares fell 1/8 to 45-3/4.
Reid has "pretty good exposure" to financial companies, especially mutual savings and loans that are only partially converted and small reinsurers.

He said these thrifts are "the last bastion of Graham and Dodd investing," referring to Ben Graham and David Dodd, who developed the modern theory of securities analysis, based on buying stocks with undervalued assets that would grow in value in the marketplace.
One standout, he said, was People's Bank-Bridgeport, Conn., which is 4.3 percent of the fund. The thrift has 41 percent of its shares publicly traded.

"It is the largest independent franchise in Connecticut, and has a healthy book of credit card business that's almost a standalone operation," he said. "It's easily the most interesting accounting you can run across."
A favorite among the niche reinsurers is Highlands Insurance Group Inc. Shares fell 1/8 to 22-1/4.
With the Russell 2000 small-cap index down 0.475 percent year to date, "we're still finding plenty of investment opportunities...," said Reid.
His universe ranges from $50 million to $1 billion in market cap, with the median stock capitalization at $300 million.
Rather than focus too deeply on quantitative measures, Reid determines values by "what a rational businessperson would be willing to pay to own an entire enterprise."
He also invests in companies with owner-oriented managers, who are looking to grow value per share rather than "trying to be bigger for the sake of being bigger."
"We think independently," he said. "We don't follow the herd. Sometimes, we tend to be little more contrarian. I don't mind that at all."
